utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was not informed about any preliminaries. Therefore, is the Prosecution ready to continue the examination of Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Ms. Hanson be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. And Ms. Bibles will now continue her examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Before we broke yesterday, you testified that in May 1992, there were an increasing number of republic-level organs formalising the Bosnian Serb state and establishing authority over other organs. Could you highlight for us the most significant of these measures as they relate to the municipal level Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first -- in late April, we have the prime minister of the government issuing instructions to Crisis Staffs. Then on the 21st and 23rd of May, the RS government is discussing abolishing Crisis Staffs to replace them with municipal war-time Presidencies. And on the 24th of May, we have the Presidency of the RS issuing instructions on the work of municipal -- war -- municipal Presidencies. Then -- I don't know where you want me to stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that the Court Officer call up 65 ter 11093.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for this document to come up, could you describe for us the 24 May 1992 instruction.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an instruction signed by Biljana Plavsic for the Presidency of the Republika Srpska, or a slightly different name at the time, on the organisation and work of Presidencies in municipalities in time of war. The first item makes it clear the dual roles of the presidents -- municipal Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it not yet on our screens yet. So what the first item is, we cannot follow that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh. I'm sorry, I have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there it is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It states that Presidencies shall be formed to organise defence activities and to establish governmental power in the municipalities. So it's establishing the state and organising defence. Number 3 says that: "The Presidencies shall provide all conditions for the work of military organs and units defending the Serbian people." As I indicate in my report, what that meant in terms of providing the conditions varied from simply supplying recruits and logistical support up to and including organising and commanding those units themselves. This instruction is also significant because of the role it emphasises for the person of the commissioner, "povjerenik," whose job is to link the highest level of the Bosnian Serb state leadership to the municipality and to ensure the constant co-ordination and implementation of the policies of the republic state organs and the Main Staff of the army. I see in the translation it just says "Main Staff of the Serbian republic" but the original is the "Main Staff of the army of the Serbian republic."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 11093.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11093 receives number P401, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Would you please take care that we get a correct translation where there are no mistakes and we'll hear about that, because we should grant leave to replace the now-uploaded translation by a new one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the relationship between the instruction we see on the screen and a subsequent decision on 31 May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of 31 May is also from the Presidency signed by Karadzic as President of the Presidency. It repeats this language from the last -- the penultimate paragraph on the work of the commissioner, it repeats this language, I believe, verbatim or at least very closely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If I could just -- I'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask at this time that the Court Officer call up 65 ter 07323.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. Could you please explain to us what's contained in this 31 May 1992 decision.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous document, as we saw, was instructions. This is an actual decision ordering the formation of municipal War Presidencies. It is essentially the same in spirit as the previous one but it's a more formal legal act, as I understand it, stating the makeup of the War Presidency, the membership, and the -- the tasks which in Article 3, as can you see, are the same as in Plavsic's instructions of the week before. And Article 4 is the same language on the work of the commissioner. This is formalising the institution of the War Presidency, so we're moving from the Crisis Staffs, which had started as party, secret party organisations but with the same membership, the same tasks, now being a formal state organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 07323.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 07323 becomes Exhibit P402, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you summarise for us the features of these measures that brought closer control of the municipal organs to the republican-level leadership.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the control is -- it's explicitly set up by the leadership, but it's the person of the commissioner here who is the link, the personal link, and he is to inform the municipal level of the policies of the leadership and ensure their implementation and he is also to inform the leadership of activities and events in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Based on your review of the materials, how effective was the role of commissioner in bringing control and communication between the municipal level and the republican level between June and December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very effective, according to those involved. At the assembly discussion at the end of 1992, when the assembly is considering whether to abolish commissioners, Krajisnik, who was the member of the Presidency responsible for the work of commissioners, praised their efforts, said that the commissioners kept him well-informed of all events in the municipality and did their work very efficiently. And, similarly, various commissioners at that assembly spoke up to say how they worked and how they reported on their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us the patterns that you observed in the relationships between the municipal-level Crisis Staffs and the Bosnian Serb leadership from May into early June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see is the Crisis Staffs and municipal War Presidencies invoking the leadership, the Presidency, and the assembly, and the government as their authority that they are -- they see themselves as part of the Bosnian Serb state, and the Bosnian Serb leadership views these organs as part of the state. They issue orders to Crisis Staffs as a category, as well as to individual Crisis Staffs. They receive reports from individual Crisis Staffs. The government extends financial support to Crisis Staffs. So they're very much operating within the framework of this Bosnian Serb state.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to now to shift direction and discuss the relationship between the municipal Crisis Staffs and the military units between April and July of 1992. Your report sets out patterns and examples of transition between the military role with the Crisis Staffs. I'd like to first address the time-period of late May of 1992. Did you observe what role, if any, military commanders had in the municipal-level Crisis Staffs or War Presidencies?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were members of the Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies, and at a minimum, the relationship was one of co-ordination and co-operation. The object of the Crisis Staff was to bring together all the forces and resources essential in the municipality, and the military was always included. And as we see, it is one of the central tasks of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: By June of 1992, what patterns did you observe with respect to the various Bosnian Serb armed forces throughout the region?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see in June is that the VRS is being established and its actual command structures and units put in place, and the Crisis Staffs that had had their own units, TO units, are seeking to integrate them into the VRS. It is not happening uniformly everywhere at the same time, but the pattern is as the army -- as the VRS gets a more robust structure, the TOs and local units are entered into it, form part of the VRS, and the Crisis Staffs are handing over the command, in those cases where they had it, of those units over to the VRS but emphasising the joint tasks and continuing co-operation, the -- and co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, going back to the more transitional time-period between April and early June of 1992, your report describes that there were differences among the municipalities based on a number of factors. Could you articulate for us what those factors would be in assessing these relationships?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic himself articulated it quite well in his assembly speech in April 1995 when he said that the Crisis Staffs formed units, sometimes with the JNA, sometimes without the JNA, sometimes in secret, hiding from the JNA, depending on who was in command. Because the JNA, at that time, still had its officer corps which was nominally -- or truly quite Communist, members of the Communist party. Wasn't always trusted everywhere. So the first element, was there even a JNA unit present in the municipality in early April or -- and did the Crisis Staff, the local Serb leadership trust that unit to act in the interests of the Serb people or not. Others, I think, it's a matter of personality. In some Crisis Staffs, we seem to see people who really enjoyed commander -- or were enthusiastic about commanding and other municipalities appear to be more hands-off, wanting a professional staff. Also, the location of the municipality itself must be different, must create different conditions. Is it right around Sarajevo or a remote outpost? And how -- and the population make-up, is it one where the Serbs are comfortably in the majority and don't feel -- and can easily change the name or intentions of the municipal government to be ruling in the interests of the Serb people, or are they a minority and more likely to be in armed conflict at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Let's now look at some of the specific municipalities from our indictment to assess how these factors actually worked on the ground in April -- between April and July of 1992. First, are you familiar with the relationship between the Crisis Staff ...

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, I have a bit of a cold.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the relationship between the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most and the military units that were in the region between April and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with several documents which indicate the evolving role. I know as early as the 1st of April, the regular army command is ordering the local commander, Basara, to establish closest possible ties in co-ordination with the local authorities which, at that time, are the Sanski Most Crisis Staff. However, there appear to have been some issues over the question of the Serbian TO which the Crisis Staff had raised and organised because I know in later April there was a meeting called to discuss their relationship. This seems to be a place, judging by the few documents that I have, where there may have been some personality differences. I know in April '95, Vlado Vrkes, member of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff in '92, is looking back and he's saying that they didn't trust Basara at the time because he was a Communist, but he told him, We're all going to be war criminals together and basically we're all -- we were all in it together. And we see by the end of May, clearly Basara is a member of the Crisis Staff and they briefing each other, co-operating on military matters, and there seems to be a seamless co-ordination there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Was this Colonel Basara who was a commander with the 6th Krajina Brigade, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's his position.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you've described that by the end of May, do you know -- or do you -- have you reviewed documents which would show which dates in May, Colonel Basara was involved in this kind of co-operation with the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have looked at many Sanski Most documents. At the moment, I can't recall them all to say exactly which meetings he was present at or not. I know -- I believe it's the 30th of May, there's a decision of the Crisis Staff setting out the tasks of everybody and including Colonel Basara in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then in subsequent meetings in the early part of June, are you aware of any documents which would indicate the relationship between Colonel Basara, the 6th Krajina Brigade and the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was present at meetings, but I'm not recalling any specific document from early June at the moment. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar -- shifting gears to Prijedor. Are you familiar with the relationship between the Crisis Staff in Prijedor and the military between April and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There we see much more harmony from the start. Shortly before the takeover in Prijedor, we do see the local leadership saying that they would ask the regular army if they were prepared to assist them in the takeover. If they weren't, the Crisis Staff was going do it anyway. But in the event, it seems to have been very close assistance at the time because we have the retrospective of Colonel Zeljaja who was a Chief of Staff of the local unit. I'm sorry, I don't know the name or number of the brigade, but he was the Chief of Staff and he boasted about providing support to the SDS, advising them on the takeover. He explains how they had a secret command. There was a public command which included Muslims, a secret command to assist the SDS. They would burn orders that they didn't like from the headquarters, including on the withdrawal of weapons, in order to assist the Serbs and a retrospective account of the takeover also praises Colonel Arsic, who was the commander of that brigade at the time, on his assistance at the takeover. So there we see clear harmony. We see in the decision on the work of the Prijedor Crisis Staff a month later repeating the instructions received from the leadership on assisting the units -- assisting the defence -- the armed forces for the defence, so I think we see a very close harmony there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Shifting now to Kljuc, are you familiar with the relationship between the Crisis Staff in Kljuc and the military and how that relationship developed between April and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Kljuc Crisis Staff was very involved before the outbreak of the conflict in forming, training, arming its own units, and the local JNA commander became alarmed that the Crisis Staff president was trying to form his own army or prevent men from serving in the regular army. But that conflict seems to have been resolved, I think, perhaps by the army changing its mind rather than the Crisis Staff, as it were. On the 13th of May, the Kljuc Crisis Staff was briefed on the decisions of the 12th of May assembly session, including the transformation of the army and the strategic objectives, and from there on, there seems to be -- there do not seem to be any conflicts in the issue of who is in charge, as it were. Although the Kljuc Crisis Staff is definitely one of the most robust and assertive ones, although they -- they state, for example, that the division would be the Crisis Staff would tell the military units what to do but would not interfere in how those orders were carried out, but they emphasise the close continuity, close harmonization. They say that no important military matters were resolved without the involvement of the Crisis Staff, that VRS commanders regularly attended the sessions and worked very closely and well. But there is a definite militarism in that Crisis Staff that even in July they're wearing combat uniforms and carrying pistols. So they seem to be one that likes a more assertive military attitude but they are working closely and, as far as I can see, without conflict with the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Looking specifically, what was the co-ordination and -- like between the local unit commanders and the -- and the municipal-level leaders by the 30th of May, 1992, in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the 30th of May, they are working together to prepare combat operations. We see in the minutes of the Crisis Staff that they're planning together and warning the civilian Serbs and planning, as far as I can see, operations together.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then by the 2nd of June, 1992, are you familiar with who was giving reports to the municipal-level leaders about the actions that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see reports from all those in charge of armed forces, the police, the TO, and the regular army, reporting to the Crisis Staff on operations. I am -- at the moment, I can't recall the name, I'm afraid, but I know it is the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with some of the actions in the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija in May of 1992 with respect to the Bosnian Serb leadership and the new VRS commander?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting in Sokolac, in Romanija, on, I believe, the 17th of May, where Krajisnik, Karadzic, and Mladic met with the leadership of both the Serbian Autonomous Region and also local municipalities including Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the time period between that meeting and the attack on Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was just a matter the days, the takeover followed a matter of days after that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with how the military and the local organs worked together during the time-periods -- from 17 May 1992 forward?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to that, we see in Rogatica a self-organised -- or a TO unit organised by the Crisis Staff, commanded by Rajko Kusic who was a member of the SDS main board, called himself commander of the Serbian TO of Rogatica. Member of the Crisis Staff, obviously, of Rogatica. And that unit appeared to be still under the Crisis Staff command as of early June. I know on the 31 May, I believe, there's an order from the VRS for operations and it specifies the forces of the Crisis Staff of Rogatica. In early June, I know Mladic noted in a report that in that region in Romanija, the integration of Crisis Staff forces into the army was proceeding slowly or not at all. The army -- excuse me, the Crisis Staff received instructions from the leadership to integrate the forces into the VRS with the establishment of the VRS, and that integration started in early June. But how -- I know from the report of the Crisis Staff of the end of June, they noted it's a process, it's taking its time, but the report stresses that the joint tasks remain the same. We will continue to support the army in everything because we have the same tasks even when the actual Crisis Staff unit is part of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sort of shifting back to the larger picture, in terms of the role of the municipal-level organs, did you see any examples in your research of a municipal Crisis Staff or War Presidency disregarding or acting against direction or instructions coming from the republican-level leadership or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw them as acting, and believing that they acted, within the instructions and guide-lines of the leadership. There are moments where they ask for clarification. There are moments of conflict with other local leaders including, like, the local army commander. But I see them as operating within -- or, I'm sorry, under the leadership of the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, finally, I'd like to direct your attention to examples that you have found of interactions between the accused and Crisis Staffs, municipal-level Crisis Staffs, in May of 1992. Where you cite intercepts in your report, have you actually listened to those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have listened to many intercepts, and I would only include them in my report if I had listened to them myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a 13 May 1992 conversation between Mladic and a person whose last name is Unkovic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a very illustrative intercept because Unkovic is first calling Gagovic, who was -- had been a JNA commander, was still the regular army commander of a unit in the Sarajevo area, and Gagovic hands the phone over to Mladic and you can hear the relief in Unkovic's voice, the joy at talking to Mladic. Mladic has just been appointed and Mladic is hitting the ground running and assuming command, and their interaction, I think, is -- shows well the relationship between the local Crisis Staffs and Mladic himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Let's back up a little bit. Who is Unkovic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ask a member of the Crisis Staff of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours -- Your Honours, I would call up 65 ter 20759. And I will ask Ms. Stewart to play this audio twice, as I understand the practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have provided transcripts to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And now, we'll play it a second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that we can have, if only on our own computers, the transcript visible? Because I see "courtroom message English" nothing at this moment. "No page currently available."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We do have hard copies we could distribute, if that would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. If you have hard copies, that's okay. If not, we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could provide hard copies, that would ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We have one more hard copy that we could provide, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is this the same -- oh, there are two here. Yes, we received two hard copies of 20759. We'll share it. One second. No, I received one of 65 ter 20810 and that's a different one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's next, Your Honour. You should also have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to follow the present one. We'll share one copy. Please play it again so that we also receive translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover]: "Gagovic: Yes. "Unkovic: Good morning. "Gagovic: Good morning. "Unkovic: Is this Colonel Gagovic? "Gagovic: Yes, it is. "Unkovic: Colonel, this is Professor Unkovic from the Crisis Staff. "Gagovic: How can I help you? "Unkovic: I just need one piece of information. "Gagovic: Yes? "Unkovic: Do you have any information on the airport? Will there be any negotiations or something like that today? "Gagovic: Negotiations over the airport today? "Unkovic: Yes. "Gagovic: There will be negotiations there but I don't know if it's going to be over the airport only, but will you be there? Who is representing your party? "Unkovic: Well, no one invited us. "Gagovic: No one invited you, eh? "Unkovic: We have decided to take the airport. "Gagovic: Pure transfer. (Talks to the people in the room). "Unkovic: And decide on it. "Gagovic: Unkovic here. (Talks to the people in the room again). "Unkovic: Yes? "Gagovic: Unkovic from Ilidza, this professor, doctor. (Talks to the people in the room and listens to what they they're telling him). Yes, your representatives will be there. But who will be there? No, I don't know who is going to be there, but there will be someone. (He listens to what the people in the room are telling him again). Here, just a moment. Hello, hello? "Unkovic: Yes? Yes? "Gagovic: Just a moment. "Mladic: Hello? "Unkovic: How can I help you? "Mladic: This is General Mladic here. How are you doing? "Unkovic: Welcome to our house. "Mladic: Thank you. May we have luck in our work. "Unkovic: May great Lord help you. "Mladic: Tell me, do you ... let me first tell you about what you're interested in. "Unkovic: Yes. "Mladic: Koljevic will come. Koljevic. "Unkovic: Mm-hm. "Mladic: Ostojic and myself will represent our side. "Unkovic: Excellent. "Mladic: There. So there is no need for you to have a representative as Ilidza. You can, however, join us and let us know about our problems there, if it is safe for you to come. The most important thing now is that all military formations, no matter who they belong to, be put under the command of the 4th Corps under Gagovic. "Unkovic: Yes?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note, we haven't finished reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you will allow us to do in cross-examination but we had two occasions to listen to the conversation and you had the transcript in front of you. Unfortunately, I have to say it, that an important statement stated by Unkovic was not entered in the transcript, so, in fact, the transcript does not reflect what is being said in the intercept. Perhaps we should have an opportunity now whilst the Prosecutor is still with the intercept, we may rehear the recording and I will draw your attention to what I am referring to. And this is an important issue which will have a serious bearing on the intercept. And you will let me know if I should do it now or perhaps you should give me guidance as to what the appropriate moment would be for me to direct your attention to this important detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to resolve this without delay. Could you already indicate where approximately the problem lies, Mr. Stojanovic? Because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet what it is, but at approximately what part of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can follow me on the transcript that we have in front of us, line 16, where the interlocutor called Unkovic says: "We have decided that the airport," and then we have three dots. And then Gagovic responds: "Pure transfer." Now in this Unkovic's answer it reads: "We have decided that the airport," and then we can hear that he says, "We have decided that we should not hand the airport over and that we will be the ones deciding about it." And this is said by someone who is a member of the Crisis Staff. This isn't part of the transcript, and it would be perhaps helpful to hear the recording again and then we can say if I'm right or not. And then I would have other issues that I would like to raise as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could play it again. And could I -- the whole procedure with our interpreters was that they would carefully follow the text. Could you focus primarily at this moment on whether there are any parts which do not appear in the transcript but words that are spoken. And I think we can stop after approximately 45 or 50 seconds because it's all in the first part, and then we'll deal with any other matter you'd like to raise, Mr. Stojanovic, after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may be helpful to play -- it's a fairly short intercept. If we could play it all the way through with the translation and then try to address the issues all at once, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then we'd need to know what other issues Mr. Stojanovic would have. Mr. Stojanovic, any other matters you would like to raise in relation to the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Other issues will be for cross-examination, Your Honour, because in the view of the Defence, this intercept is precisely one of the examples that illustrate the relationship between Mladic and the Crisis Staff, in terms of the powers that the Crisis Staff members believed that they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other issues are about the interpretation and how to understand this conversation. We now focus, then, exclusively on the accuracy of the transcript. Could it be played again, and I think we can stop approximately halfway when we have gone past this part. Perhaps where Koljevic comes in -- where at least Koljevic is mentioned as someone who was present during the meeting. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I also, while I was reading, I missed the -- the comment by the interpreters that they had not yet finished reading. So we'll then perhaps play the whole again, and then wait patiently until you have finished the interpretation, which, of course, is quite understandable that you cannot follow the speed of speech. So we'll replay it entirely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, but weren't the interpreters supposed to listen to the relevant part before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that's the best. Let's -- we play it first half, then we stop at approximately where Koljevic is mentioned. And then we might later, after we have discussed this part, continue with the remainder so that we have the whole of the translation on the transcript, if that is a good way to proceed. I'm looking at the interpreters and it seems that they agree. So we first play the first half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there portions which are not transcribed? And I think the focus is on the airport, approximately on from the 20th second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Unkovic, instead of what is written in the transcript, "We have decided to take the airport," in fact says, "We have decided not to give the airport."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything else there which is not transcribed? The next we hear -- we see is: "Pure transfer." And then: "Talks to people in the room." Is there any -- is that audible? Is that complete?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's not audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not audible. And perhaps the ... and then the next which is transcribed is Unkovic: "And decide on it." Which, as a stand-alone few words, is not easy to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was an overlap between Unkovic and Gagovic and, in fact, Unkovic says: "We have decided not to give the airport and we shall be the ones deciding about it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the gist of what Unkovic says is that: We're the ones and we have decided not to give it. Is that, Mr. Stojanovic, what you'd like to point at?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. In view of the fact that I know the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Bibles, we'll need a new transcript anyhow. That may be clear. Now, in order to have the latter part of the transcript translated to us, I suggest that we start on from where we stopped and that we'll then wait until full translation has -- appears on our today's transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover]: "Mladic: Ostojic and myself will represent our side. "Unkovic: Excellent. "Mladic: There. So there is no need for you to have a representative as Ilidza. You can, however, join us and let us know about your problems there, if it is safe for you to come. The most important thing now is that all military formations, no matter who they belong to, be put under the command of the 4th Corps under Gagovic. "Unkovic: Yes? "Mladic: All this. Units shall be filled with men, formed organised, and everything must be all right. "Unkovic: Excellent. "Mladic: Have you understood me? "Unkovic: Yes. "Mladic: I'll give you further instructions when we get together. "Unkovic: Excellent. "Mladic: There. "Unkovic: One more question. "Mladic: Yes? "Unkovic: We have some of Arkan's Men here. "Mladic: Yes? "Unkovic: Are they under our command? "Mladic: All are. All under arms are under my command if they want to keep their heads on their shoulders. "Unkovic: Excellent. Excellent. "Mladic: So all shall be under our command. No one shall do things on their own, and the five-day cease-fire must be observed. "Unkovic: Yes. "Mladic: But in case they attack you, approach you, then you will destroy them. "Unkovic: Of course. "Mladic: There. "Unkovic: Sure thing. Thank you, General. "Mladic: Have a good one. "Unkovic: Have a good one. "Mladic: Bye."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, your report details other intercepts and other communications with the accused and Crisis Staffs. Could you tell us whether the communications between the commander of the VRS and the Crisis Staff levels heard in those conversations, are they consistent with your observations on the relationship between the VRS and Crisis Staffs in the early Bosnian Serb state?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because my conclusions were based on evidence such as that intercept, those intercepts. We see Mladic, when he feels necessary, getting on the phone and ordering Crisis Staff members. In the case of the other intercept - you have the transcript of it - in Trnovo, ordering a Crisis Staff member into a military operation. In this one we heard it more an advising, but he is clearly, yeah, when necessary, asserting authority and dealing with these municipal Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that we're at or past the break time. Would this be a good time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your estimate was one hour, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It is. And I'm very much at the end of that. I will have just a few minutes when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Few minutes. Then we'll take a break and -- after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- while we wait for the witness to come in, I will tender 65 ter 20759 or -- if we have it MFI'd so that once we correct the translation, we can move for a formal admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not only translation but transcription as well. But any objection against it being MFI'd? Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 20759 receives Exhibit P403 [Realtime transcript read in error “P402”], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Finally, Ms. Hanson, I will ask you if you could summarise for us the nature of the relationship that you have observed in your research between General Mladic and the municipal organs in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not look at that specifically as I started my research long before I was involved in it -- for Mladic, so the documents I do see show that once he was appointed as commander of the Bosnian Serb army, Mladic met with a number of people at the regional and municipal level. He did not have a lot of direct contact but, of course, he is at the highest level himself, but I certainly see that the municipal level saw him as the commander of the armed forces, and although there may have been some local jealousies and possessiveness about their units, they saw themselves and Mladic as sharing joint tasks and joint goals and working together in the defence of Serbian interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did he -- did his appointment appear to have an impact on those municipalities which had been developing their own armies?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only place where I can really connect his appointment to -- to a local effect is in Kljuc where they were briefed, as I say, the day after on his appointment. Whether it's his appointment itself or simply the course of development of the army of the Bosnian Serbs or not, it's -- what I definitely see as the trend over May and June is the integration of these locally formed units into the army structure and a recognition of the command structure of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I am, Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, once Mr. Stojanovic has found his materials, he'll cross-examine you. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for the Prosecution -- for the Defence of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stojanovic switch on another microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will be putting a few questions to you in relation to your report. But before we move on to the documents specifically, I would like us briefly to go through your CV. It was my understanding that you do not have any legal training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will we agree that in your written report that you entitled: "Crisis Staffs, War Presidencies, and War Commissions," for the most part you dealt with the legal and normative framework regulating the question of Crisis Staffs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was the most part of my report, no. I do look at those, the normative documents, but a great deal of my report is concerning the documents of the Crisis Staff themselves and what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As for this report, did any lawyers help you draw the conclusions that have to do with the legal framework within which the Crisis Staffs functioned and operated?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This work and its conclusions are all my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you wrote this report, you were a staff member at the OTP. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For many years now, you've been working as an analyst of documents in the OTP, documents that are being made available to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Technically I'm a research officer not an analyst. But it's very much what I'm doing is analysing documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So I would be right if I were to say that it's not only that you research documents but you analyse them as well; is that correct? Also you draw certain conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would group research and analysis very much together, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Over the years while you've been working, it was my understanding that you learnt B/C/S. So you are familiar with B/C/S and you can even use the Cyrillic alphabet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with B/C/S and I can use Cyrillic, but I learned it long before I started working here. And I was hired because of my knowledge of B/C/S. Not that I learned it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For a while, you worked in Belgrade as a researcher attached to the then-Army of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not attached to the army. I was a Fulbright scholar funded by the US government to do research for my dissertation. My research was conducted in the military historical institute of the JNA, but I did not -- I was not attached to the JNA. I was simply working in the archives of the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me whether at any point in time during your stay in the then-Yugoslavia and in Belgrade you had any kind of previous knowledge about Mr. Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall now. I may have read of him in the newspapers in -- in April or May 1992, but I certainly do not recall any specific knowledge at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically who entrusted this task to you, to work out this analysis?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it was the team for prosecuting Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic. However, I was not specifically briefed by any member of that team. I was briefed by the then-head of my team, the Leadership Research Team. So he must have spoken to the lawyers on the Krajisnik-Plavsic team and then came to me and explained that I was to research Crisis Staffs. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you get any tasks at any point in time to testify as an expert in the trial of Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the summer, I believe it was, I can't remember, maybe it was earlier in the spring, I was told that I would be testifying in this case. So fairly recently. And I was asked if I wanted to make any changes to my report. At that time I didn't -- I was not asked to do any further research. I simply made a few corrections on my report. But I was tasked as a Crisis Staff expert many years before this trial started, or before I was told that I would be involved in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you get any order or instruction in writing as to what your expert report in the Ratko Mladic case should contain? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not have any specific tasks as a staff member of the OTP and an expert at the same time that pertained to the case of Ratko Mladic. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one minor one in the early days before I was identified as an expert, I was asked to take a look at the section of the pre-trial brief dealing with Crisis Staffs because it had been taken essentially from the Karadzic brief, as I understood. I just cast my eye on it, but it was based again on my contribution to the Karadzic case. Once I realised that I would be an expert witness, I was removed from any contact, further contact with the team, and no other taskings. From the Mladic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, the entire text of the expert report that we have before us, except for your remarks in paragraph 10 of your report, is identical to the text that you prepared for the Prosecution case against Radovan Karadzic. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, my remarks in paragraph 10 are not changed. I wish I had read them more carefully and I would have changed those remarks. What -- I changed a few words, including the unfortunate omission of the word "not" but it is -- except for perhaps four changes, minor in the sense of a word or two, it is identical to the Karadzic text. And I did not do any further original research for this between Karadzic and -- for -- for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that you did not make any changes in the text except for these four very minor changes, as you said, from the Karadzic case up until the Ratko Mladic case, did you carry out a further analysis of the documents that were accessible to you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am always looking at the documents -- any new documents coming into me or reviewing other ones, but I did not conduct for this report or this testimony any specific research.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So I would be right if I say that technically, from the point of view of the text of this report, and also in terms of the documents that are accompanying your report, you do not have any alterations or adjustments in relation to what did you in the Karadzic case. You did not change this in any way to adapt to the Mladic case. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would be right also if I were to say that it would basically be the identical expert report that you provided in terms of your assignment related to the two cases before this international criminal court. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two cases meaning Karadzic and Mladic? Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please help me resolve another question and that is related to the documents that you used in your report. This is what I'm asking you: In your database that the OTP made available to you, over all of these years while you worked here, did the OTP make available to you the documents of all the Crisis Staffs in Republika Srpska or only the documents of a certain number of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had at my disposal all the documents in the possession of the OTP. That body of evidence is limited by what the OTP collected or received, so I certainly do not have all the documents of all the Crisis Staffs in Republika Srpska. That simply is not the case. But I had the free use of anything in the possession of the OTP, which included, for some municipalities, extensive documents of Crisis Staffs; for many municipalities, very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will we agree that there weren't any documents whatsoever from certain municipalities in relation to the constitution and operation of the Crisis Staffs as such?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For some municipalities, there were no documents that I could find.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, during the direct examination you said that during your research you came across documents that were exculpatory in your view. Would you tell the Trial Chamber how you made that assessment? What it was that would be exculpatory in the documents that you had.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exculpatory are documents that indicate somebody -- another individual or group was responsible for crimes. It would also be exculpatory if I saw that crimes were investigated and prosecuted. I know that a lot of Defences like to have documents that show the other side was also conducting similar activities so I would note that. I was not researching whether Crisis Staffs themselves were guilty or innocent. That isn't the issue. The issue is what Crisis Staffs were doing. So there were certainly plenty of documents which showed Crisis Staffs were also acting as ordinary municipal governments but that isn't exculpatory or inculpatory. It is simply they were doing other things as well. But we would receive guide-lines on what is considered exculpatory for each case and in general it's -- anything that would be looked at as helpful to the Defence would be noted in -- and passed on to lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But my key question would be the following: On the basis of what level of your knowledge do you assess whether a document is -- is exculpatory or not, in view of the answer you've provided, stating that you do not have -- you have not had any legal training?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't make that assessment. I flag it. I pass it on to lawyers to make that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then, on the basis of their assessment whether something is exculpatory or not in terms of the documents that you studied, analysed, and flagged, do they ultimately decide what is exculpatory? Ultimately, out of all of that.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a lawyer's job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these documents, after such an assessment, were provided to this Defence team of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the details of disclosure at all, but I trust that I've done my bit and the rest of the OTP is doing their duty. I don't know the details of disclosure, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to conclude my questions on this topic with the following: Over all these years, did you have the physical possibility of visiting the areas of Kljuc, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Sarajevo, Zvornik, Bratunac? That is to say, the municipalities that you dealt with the most on the basis of your report, or, rather, their Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not been to Kljuc or Sanski Most. I have been to Prijedor, Sarajevo, Zvornik. I have not been to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask us to take a look at P379 together in e-court. This is a report -- or, rather, this is the report that you compiled. So let us focus on paragraph 4. Then I'm going to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be more convenient for you to have a hard copy of your report there, because I see you staring there at your screen, which is not always easy to -- then I take it that the Defence would have no objection against providing a hard copy to the witness. If you have one -- the one who is first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So it is paragraph 4, Ms. Hanson. In the second sentence of this paragraph, you say, in terms of Crisis Staffs, you say that they: "... supported armed units in the municipalities. They supported, enabled and, in some cases, directed the armed units in the municipalities." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what my question is: At the time when the Crisis Staffs functioned, appreciating the terms that you referred to during your direct examination, what is it that you mean when you say "armed units"? Who is that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicate, there's a variety of armed units. Some of them are the regular army. That is the former JNA still in place in Bosnia. Some of them are locally raised TO units. Sometimes part of the formal TO structure. Sometimes secretly formed in armed units calling themselves Serbian TO. As I've indicated in my report, by the time we can speak of armed units of the VRS itself, the Crisis Staffs command abilities are shrinking or disappearing, and those units are part of the VRS structure. It is very important to talk about which time-period as -- as I said in my report and in my testimony. So if we're talking about April, we see much more assertiveness by Crisis Staffs over armed units than we see in late May or June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I'd like to ask you. When you listed everything that you considered to be armed units, is it your general conclusion that you're drawing here in paragraph 4 that such a heterogenous structure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 is in the executive summary, which, of course, loses a lot of details and doesn't give much information about what it's really about. Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber would consider it that -- considers that it would be better assisted by going into the -- the -- the real report rather than what may serve as a kind of general introduction so that you know, more or less, what will follow. Executive summaries are not -- do not contain the proper analysis of what is found in the report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will take this on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say, as you sit here today, that such heterogenous structures of units that were active out in the field in Bosnia-Herzegovina had the same status before the Crisis Staffs, both in terms of the JNA, paramilitary formations, Territorial Defence elements, and local units established locally?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say the same status before the crisis units, you mean did the crisis units have the same level of authority over all of them. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I want to ask you about it. Was the level of control exerted by the Crisis Staffs equal in all these cases? And if we can, let us place it in the context of the time-periods.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not conclude that the status was equal for all those sorts of units, either in -- over time or discussing the various kinds of units or in various areas of Republika Srpska. I do not claim that it was all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can differentiate between them, I would invite you to do so and to tell Their Honours what the distinction is based on.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the distinction is based on the evidence I find, the documents. Obviously the regular army, the late JNA, had its own command structure. I see the local -- the commander of any local regular army units being a member of the Crisis Staff and co-ordinating operations with the Crisis Staff, but I see in some cases the president of the Crisis Staff being the commander of a locally formed unit. So it's a very different relationship, for example. And paramilitaries, we see the Crisis Staffs inviting them, arming them, creating them, and sometimes -- claim -- putting them under the control of the Crisis Staff but not a correct command or simply paying them and giving them tasks. So it is various levels of control and co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us then try and agree chronologically. Can you tell Their Honours when the Army of Republika Srpska was established?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20 -- 21st, I believe, of May, was the decision on the establishment, although at the assembly session on the 12th of May -- no, Mladic was appointed as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And up until what point were Crisis Staffs formally functioning? Bearing in mind the documents that you referred to and that were shown to you by my learned friend during the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, the presidential decision of 31 May says Crisis Staffs ceased to operate. But as I make clear in my report, in practical terms that was not the case everywhere. Far from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if we can agree, and if we observe the formalism that we referred to as far as the terms are concerned, and we will speak about what it is that the Crisis Staffs grow out into, on the 21st of May, the Army of Republika Srpska became operational, and ten days later, the 31st of May, Crisis Staffs cease to exist. Is that correct, that there is an overlap of ten days between them?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it difficult to observe the formalism when the documents show that the formalism was not observed. But if we're going simply by these formal decrees, yes, there's an overlap of ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And we will agree that after the 31st of May, someone else, those who took over the powers of the Crisis Staff, had a new relationship with the newly established VRS, is that right? And in fact, we are going to be discussing them precisely.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not someone else. The people who were on the Crisis Staffs became the War Presidencies. It's a seamless -- a seamless transition from Crisis Staff to War Presidency where we even see that change of name. So it's not someone else at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But am I right in saying that this isn't about semantics only, because you did refer to the decision by Radovan Karadzic introducing the construct of commissioners. You drew upon this to say that this marked the formation of -- of closer ties between the newly established War Presidency and the republican authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The decision by Karadzic did not introduce the construct of commissioners. We see that as early as 26 April, the instructions by Branko Djeric. It's the 24 May instructions from Biljana Plavsic that first really explicate the commissioners, so I don't say that Karadzic introduced it. But I do say that the person of the commissioners created a personal tie between the municipal authorities and the republican.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the case that formally the commission was established as an institution in the decision published in the official journal of the Assembly of Republika Srpska on the 31st of May, 1992? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The commissions were formed by the decision of the 10th of June. The 31 May is Presidency, "predsednistvo." The 10th of June is commission, "povjerenistvo."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We will agree that before the 31st of May, you didn't find anywhere in your research that the War Presidency had been established and commissioners appointed. All these decisions date post-31st May. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I do note some places where there were War Presidencies before the 31st of May, and I'll have to check my document, but I believe in Foca there may have been reference to a commissioner before the 31st of May. But I'm not certain about that one. But I agree that the 31st of May decision establishes War Presidencies to be the formal term for these municipal collective emergency bodies. Some places we see War Presidencies before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will proceed. Staying with the same document, P379, let us look at paragraph 20, where you speak of the formation of the Crisis Staffs, pursuant to the instruction on the organisation and operation of the organs of -- of Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a state of emergency, dated the 19th December 1991. This is my question: Based on your research, who authored these instructions? Who issued the instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorship is not clear. It is issued by the leadership of the SDS. On the first page, it says: "Main Board of the SDS." The last page says: "SDS Crisis Staff." The relationship between those two is not clear. But it was distributed by the SDS leadership. The actual authorship is not known.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you this precisely because of my next question. Although you stated as much in your written report, you say in the latter part of paragraph 20 that the fact that these instructions state that they were made by the SDS Crisis Staff, you say that it was one of the first indications of the existence of a Crisis Staff at a republican level. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. But what I say in the original is slightly different and it gives a different nuance. It is an early indication of a republic-level Crisis Staff. I do not claim that there was constantly one republic-level Crisis Staff but I see mention of one at various times in 1991 and 1992. So this is -- the fact that it is signed by the SDS BiH Crisis Staff indicates there was a Crisis Staff, apparently, at this time. But I'm not saying the -- it was translated back as "the" and I just want to emphasise that I'm not claiming there was one identifiable republic-level Crisis Staff constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I must admit that I fail to understand what you're saying. Are you referring now to the republican-level Crisis Staff with reference to Republika Srpska only or in terms of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point I'm talking about SDS. This is before the formation of the Republika Srpska. I'm talking about an SDS republican-level Crisis Staff. But, in fact, I avoid talking about such a thing in my report. There are a few indications, references to such a thing, but I don't have enough to claim -- I'm very far from claiming that there was some permanent such -- or established such body. Honestly, I think part of the -- our misunderstanding just is in the translation from B/C/S without an article to the English question of definite or indefinite article. That may be part of the trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To overcome this problem, let us look at document 65 ter 28386, 28386 in e-court, which is precisely the document we have been referring to, the instructions for the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a state of emergency issued in Sarajevo on the 19th of December, 1991. Let us stay with the cover page for now. The preamble states that it is a document issued by the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically its Main Board. Was this the text that made you say that the document was issued by the Main Board of the SDS, as you put it in paragraph 20 of your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This cover page, yes, say it's from the Main Board. And I have many, many references from the Crisis Staffs formed saying that they were formed on the instructions of the Main Board. So they perceived the instructions as coming from the Main Board, and the instructions themselves state "Main Board."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page of the text, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You then went onto establish that -- at the end of the text, it reads: "SDS Crisis Staff." Hence, my question. Did your study at any point - and based on a document, and if so, which - establish that December of 1991 there existed a Crisis Staff at the level of the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the only reference I'm familiar with to such a high level SDS Crisis Staff in December 1991. I have other references from other times. This is the only one I have from December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As an analyst, did you draw a conclusion based on this that there did, nevertheless, exist a Crisis Staff in December of 1991? Because we have both the signature and stamp and the author missing.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm reluctant to draw a conclusion of any importance that there was such a Crisis Staff in operation. There may have been a small group that called itself a Crisis Staff. But, no, on the basis of one -- one little -- one reference, I'm not going to draw any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on to the next paragraph. Can we go back to your report again. Paragraph 21. Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit 379. There, you say, analysing these instructions, that in Variant A the laws of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were supposed to no longer be followed and the orders of parallel Serb authorities was supposed to be followed instead. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you make such a generalised statement in your expert report, it is my duty to ask you as follows. Which are the laws that under Variant A the Crisis Staffs were supposed to stop abiding by and which had been adopted in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we see many declarations in this time in late 1991 from various SDS bodies that they will stop abiding by any SRBiH laws that are not in accordance with the federal constitution. But the formation of separate police stations and secret arming is presumably not in accordance with SRBiH law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think we have come to the crucial issue now. Let us look at the instructions. This is 28386. This is the 65 ter number of the document. I think we have it before us. Please look at item 1 on page 1 in both versions, which reads -- the following page. It reads, item 1 -- it's the very next page. I would call it the preamble of the document, which reads: "These instructions are being issued due to justified suspicion that certain forces are working persistently, thoroughly and in an organised manner to remove Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia, and thereby also its Serbian people. It elaborates the unified tasks, measures and other activities that will be undertaken within the national community of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the aim of implementing the plebescite decision of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina to live in a single state, both in the existing conditions and circumstances, and in all those that may arise, bearing in mind the development of the overall political and security situation." My question is: We're talking about December of 1991, the time when the instructions were issued. Was this the point in time that was described in item 1? Or, to put it more simply, was this the point in time when we had a clearly expressed will of the three constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was completely different in terms of whether they should continue living together in a single state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how clearly expressed the will of the three constituent peoples could be said -- whether we can say that the will was clearly expressed at this point in December 1991. The plebescite had been held only for Serbs with different questions for non-Serbs, and very few non-Serbs participated. The elections had been held two year -- a year earlier for a different purpose, for the -- not for the -- I mean, for the Assembly of Bosnia, but not expressly on the issue of the future in a single state. It was certainly a -- there was an ongoing discussion on the future of Bosnia at this time and the future of Yugoslavia. Obviously that's true. But I hesitate on your expression of the clearly expressed will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me, then, to avoid the field of semantics and ask you instead: As an analyst, was this period of time - and I mean December 1991 - one where -- when there was a decision expressed by the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina at a referendum not to leave the country that they had been living in until that point? That's to say, Yugoslavia. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was such a plebescite in November, yes. And the overwhelming majority was a yes vote to stay in -- for -- in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And will you agree with me when I say that four and a half months later, the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina took the decision to step out of Yugoslavia and start the procedure of establishing the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a referendum at the end of February for all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which the vote was for the independence of Bosnia. But I'd say it was the leadership that took the decision to step out. But, yes, there was a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now this is what I'm asking you, bearing in mind these two absolutely divergent decisions that were plebiscitary, according to the then-constitution of Yugoslavia, was it possible to carry out a cessation that would have been based on the constitution and law, for it to be legal?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a constitutional lawyer at all. No expert. There were many discussions at the very highest levels on how it could be resolved. And if they couldn't resolve it, I certainly am not going to offer any analysis of the constitution, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber gets the impression that you're attempting to elicit from this expert witness a judgement on whether this was right or wrong or constitutional or legal or whatever. Now, I do not think that the witness in her report has stated any of such thing, and I think wisely has not done it because she does not claim to be a legal expert. Apart from that, the way in which you phrase the questions about plebescites, et cetera, would need a thorough analysis of those aspects. That is not what this witness tasked herself with, and she has not analysed that. So, therefore, the Chamber wonders whether this is a line of questioning which assists the Chamber and whether we could reasonably expect the witness to assist the Chamber in the matters the Chamber will have to determine. At the same time, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break. We'll take that break but could first the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move on, I have one item. On the transcript it appears as if document 20759 has been assigned Exhibit P402, where it certainly was meant, whether the Registrar misspoke or whether it was recorded wrongly, that this document was MFI'd under number P403, and we're talking about the intercepted telephone conversation between Professor Unkovic, Colonel Miroslav Gagovic and General Ratko Mladic. And the other matter, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, that resolves one question. Before we move forward if I could just posit a question. Yesterday Your Honours ruled on our request with respect to bar table motions for expert witnesses, at T4139, lines 18 to 21, you directed that a party calling an expert witness may tender materials underlying the report after the witness testifies and has been cross-examined. And particular issues have been challenged. I just want to clarify whether in the Chamber's view we need to tender any such documents on re-examination or whether, if appropriate, some of those documents could be the subject of a subsequent bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider your question over the break, Ms. Bibles. And we take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. The witness had asked during the break whether she could fetch some materials you'd like to consult. The Chamber gave permission for her to do so. But just to go to her office and then take them out, without any further discussions. Later on, the Chamber was informed that the witness would like to have available to her the 19th of December instructions, and Madam Registrar has offered, because they are, of course, known in the e-court under a 65 ter number, offered to print them out for the witness, and I invited Madam Registrar to do so. Just to keep you updated on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And also I have to give some guidance, Ms. Bibles, on your question. One second, Ms. Hanson. If there's any challenge to the conclusions of an expert witness referring to source materials and if such source materials are used by the opposing party, then, as we indicated, first of all, that it's allowed to get to those source materials with the expert witness and then for the Prosecution to -- to seek admission of -- of relevant material as well. Now, if that material, as such, that questions should be put to the witness about those materials, then - and that's the preferred way - do it during re-examination. If, however, you would say, these five documents to which the expert couldn't say anything, at least we're not aware of her being familiar with those documents, but they shed light on the issue raised in cross-examination, then upon a clear announcement that you wish to tender five or seven or ten documents shedding additional light on the matter raised during cross-examination, then we would not exclude for the possibility that you would then be allowed to make a bar table motion specific on that subject and then tender those documents in that way. But we expected usually you would like to use those with the witness and then it's best done in re-examination. Then, Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.
